messages.author: 7edfe2ae4a1e4b1d
messages.subject: Speed while running logistics regression
parts:
Hi:

I am trying to run a standard logistics regression with Stan, however it takes me several hours to just get first 200 samples from the posterior distribution. Could anybody give me some idea how to speed up my model ?

The data have around 20K obs with 3 predictors. But even if I tried first 1000 obs in my data, stan still draw samples slowly. 

Best,

Yilong

messages.subject: Re: Speed while running logistics regression
parts:
Speaking as a person who has only a few days of experience with stan, and thus could be completely wrong in what I say, you may find it faster to use a model matrix than to use individual columns.  It will also have the effect of expressing all the predictor columns as real.  Right now you have mixture of integer and real columns, which is going to force conversions in every evaluation of the linear predictor.

I'm not sure how the R interface works yet but I guess I would start by fitting the glm then extracting the model matrix and seeing if I could pass that as a stan matrix type.  (Well, actually I would start by plotting the data which shows that the effect of age is not linear but more like a "hockey stick".  Before converting "gay", "gender", and "race" to indicators try

messages.author: 0839befa8a8b7d53
messages.subject: Re: Speed while running logistics regression
parts:
I think the problem is that you have the [N] instead of [n] in your GLM expression.

So instead of:
gay[n] ~ bernoulli_logit( alpha + beta1*age[N]+beta2*gender[N]+b*race1[N] + h*race2[N] + o*race3[N]);

You want:
gay[n] ~ bernoulli_logit( alpha + beta1*age[n]+beta2*gender[n]+b*race1[n] + h*race2[n] + o*race3[n]);

Even if that wasn't causing the sluggishness, it will fix a serious inference problem.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Speed while running logistics regression
parts:
On Monday, October 8, 2012 8:49:32 AM UTC-4, Yilong wrote:
I am trying to run a standard logistics regression with Stan, however it takes me several hours to just get first 200 samples from the posterior distribution. Could anybody give me some idea how to speed up my model ?

In general about speed, make sure that you allow the C++ compiler to fully optimize. This can be done from rstan by specifying set_cppo(mode = "fast") or by setting up a Makevars file (see http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-admin.html#Customizing-package-compilation or https://code.google.com/p/stan/wiki/RStanGettingStarted )

A minor thing, you define a parameter p that is not used in the model.

Major thing: if possible use a vectorized density rather than looping over the observations. So your original

model {
  for (n in 1:N)

gay[n] ~ bernoulli_logit( alpha + beta1*age[N]+beta2*gender[N]+b*race1[N] + h*race2[N] + o*race3[N]);
}

(also what Richard said is correct: you would use [n] instead of [N] if you had to do a loop)

becomes

model {
  // possibly put priors on parameters here
  gay ~ bernoulli_logit( alpha + beta1*age + beta2*gender +b*race1 + h*race2 + o*race3 );
}

Except, at the moment that doesn't quite work when the variables are defined as arrays, so I had to make them vectors, as in

data {
  int <lower=0> N;
  int <lower=0,upper=1> gay[N];
  vector[N] age;
  vector[N] race1;
  vector[N] race2;
  vector[N] race3;
  vector[N] gender;
}

What Doug suggested is correct, and although I don't think it makes a huge difference in speed, it does make the code clearer. Assuming you define such a NxK model matrix in R and call it X, the code would simply be

data {
  int <lower=0> N;
  int <lower=1> K;
  int <lower=0,upper=1> gay[N];
  matrix[N,K] X;
}
parameters {
  vector[K] coeffs;
}
model {
  // possibly put priors on coeffs here
  gay ~ bernoulli_logit( X * coeffs );
}

I am attaching a .R file with all my modifications. On my computer, it still looks like it would take many minutes (I didn't wait that long), but certainly not hours.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speed while running logistics regression
parts:
You should be able to follow Doug's advice to
switch the data to reals and put everything in
a matrix, and then use the vectorized version of
bernoulli_logit. That and eliminating an unused parameter
should make everything much faster.

Unfortunately, we don't have constraints on a column by
column basis, so you might want to leave your data
declared with constraints as you have:

data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0,upper=1> gay[N];

real<lower=0,upper=130> age[N];
int<lower=0,upper=1> race1[N];
int<lower=0,upper=1> race2[N];
int<lower=0,upper=1> race3[N];
int<lower=0,upper=1> gender[N];
}

and add a new block constructing the data matrix:

transformed data {
matrix[N,7] x;

for (n in 1:N) {
x[1] = 1.0; // intercept
x[2] = gay[N];
...
x[7] = gender[N]; // you probably mean "sex" here, not "gender"
}
}

Next, the parameters need to be reworked. First, get rid of the
parameter p you don't use (I'm assuming this is a holdover from
BUGS-style intermediate variable coding). Unused parameters like this can slow
down sampling because they subtly affect the posterior geometry by
adding a new dimension that's not highly constrained by the model.
This can affect the U-turn condition on sampling. It also takes time
to do the transform and auto-dif. So replace:


parameters {
real<lower=0, upper=1> p; // this one you don't use, and it could slow down sampling
real alpha;
real beta1;
real beta2;
real b;
real h;
real o;
}

with:

parameters {
vector[7] beta;
}

and then replace the model:

model {
for (n in 1:N)
gay[n] ~ bernoulli_logit( alpha + beta1*age[N]+beta2*gender[N]+b*race1[N] + h*race2[N] + o*race3[N]);
}

with the vectorized version:

model {
gay ~ bernoulli_logit(x * beta);
}

Then if you really want reports on the individual params,
you originally declared, you could declare and define them
in a generated quantities block.

- Bob

As Jiqiang pointed out that comment is in reference to the URL in the file logistic.stat.R included in the original posting.

There is another subtle point with respect to the stability of parameters in a model such as this.  As in many such data sets the categories of the 'race' variable are highly unbalanced.  About 80% of the respondents are white.  There is a slight advantage in rearranging the order of the labels so that white is the reference category.  The parameters being estimated are then, for example, the difference between white and Hispanic rather than black and Hispanic.

(I also tend to reorder the levels of "gender", which in this case is actually "sex", not "gender", as "Male", "Female" because I use lattice graphics frequently and the first category is a blue (cyan actually) color and the second a pink (magenta actually) and it is easy to remember blue for boys and pink for girls.)

You can accomplish the relabeling by
> data$race <- relevel(data$race, "White")
